newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Germany sceptical of Austrian border controls.
newsitem.headline: Germany sceptical of Austrian border controls.

text.p: As the era of control-free travel within the European Union looms, Austria has yet to convince its neighbour Germany about its ability to police its outer borders against the growing number of illegal immigrants.
Austria is due on July 1 to join the Schengen group of seven EU countries, including Germany, which have agreed on a system of open borders and passport-free movement.
But with continuing unrest in the Balkans and widespread poverty in Turkey and former East bloc countries, more emigrants are heading west in search of fortune and security.
Austria, on the EU's frontline with the east, offers a perfect gateway. Its border with former East bloc countries is 1,260 km (790 miles) long.
The country seized over 10,000 illegal immigrants in 1996, a rise of 61 percent from 1995, according to a recent interior ministry report.
In January this year customs police arrested 784 refugees -- 317 found hidden in vehicles and 323 trying to cross the border on foot.
Guenther Beckstein, interior minister of Germany's southern province Bavaria which borders Austria, has repeatedly voiced concern about a possible influx of refugees when borders open.
"I am extremely worried that many people will try to come to Bavaria through Austria," he said in a recent interview with Austrian state television.
He favours delaying Austrian membership of Schengen and opening up the border step by step.
"I think it is wrong to put ourselves under time pressure which will speed things up at the cost of security requirements," he continued.

Austria stepped up border security last month after Bavarian border police discovered 41 ethnic Albanians from Kosovo and 52 Turks concealed in lorries, which had successfully passed through Austrian checks.
Austrian border police are now using carbon dioxide probes which detect human breath to check for human smuggling.
Oskar Strohmeyer, in charge of border police at the Austrian interior ministry, dismissed German fears about Austria's readiness for Schengen.
"We are well on track," he told Reuters. Some 2.7 billion schillings ($225 million) had been put towards preparation for joining the agreement, he noted.

It was pointless to compare police effectiveness on different sides of the border, he said. "To say, 'I've caught three lorries today and you've only got one' doesn't help anyone. We're interested in cooperation."
Austrian border controls are due to be examined by a committee of Schengen participants in April.

France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain, Portugal and Germany are all full Schengen members. Greece, Italy and Austria have signed the accord but have yet to put the required legislation into place.
